statements.text: A generated image or paragraph is assembled from patterns learned across many examples rather than copied from one source file.
statements.explanation: The model stores statistical regularities, not a library of files. It produces output by predicting what fits the prompt, which blends patterns from countless sources. Close copies of heavily repeated material can still occur, which is why checking for them matters.

statements.text: A generated image is a collage of pieces cut and pasted from existing pictures.
statements.explanation: Image models learn how shapes, textures, and captions relate, then produce new pixels from noise guided by the prompt. No stored images are stitched together. The result can resemble training images when a style or subject was heavily represented, but the mechanism is generation, not assembly.

statements.text: Generative AI has surpassed human creativity, producing more original work than people working alone.
statements.explanation: Large comparisons of people with and without AI help found no meaningful creativity gap. What changed was the spread of ideas: AI-assisted groups converged on similar outputs. Creativity in the sense of surprising, fitting, original work remains a human-led activity.

statements.text: Studies comparing people with and without AI help found no large creativity gap, and AI use made the group's ideas more alike.
statements.explanation: Individuals with AI did about as well as those without, while the pool of ideas lost variety. The practical lesson is to use the model to widen your options and then push past its first suggestions rather than accept them.

statements.text: Idea diversity increases when everyone on a team uses the same AI tool for brainstorming.
statements.explanation: The opposite shows up in research: shared tools pull people toward the same likely ideas, a homogenization effect. Teams get more variety by brainstorming alone first, then using the model to extend and challenge the list, not to produce it.

statements.text: A model's suggestions tend to cluster around common ideas, so asking for many options and the unusual ones yields more variety.
statements.explanation: The most likely continuation is, by definition, the most typical one. Asking for twenty ideas, or for ideas a cautious person would reject, pushes the model off its default. You then choose, which is where the creative judgment lives.

statements.text: Asking a model for its single best idea produces a better result than asking it for many ideas.
statements.explanation: The single answer is the most typical answer, and typical is rarely what creative work needs. A long list exposes the range, and the odd items at the end are often the most useful. Generate wide, then select narrow.

statements.text: Asking a model to explore several directions before committing produces more varied drafts than asking for one answer.
statements.explanation: Techniques such as Tree of Thought have the model branch, evaluate, and only then continue. For creative work the same shape applies: three openings, three tones, three structures, then a choice. The branching is cheap; the choice is yours.

statements.text: Describing a style, such as a plain-spoken field guide or a noir voice-over, changes the form of the output while the content request stays the same.
statements.explanation: Style prompting separates what to say from how to say it. The model has seen many examples of each style and can shape sentence length, vocabulary, and rhythm to match. Check that the style did not swallow the facts.

statements.text: A model can write in the manner of a well-known author because it learned patterns from text by and about them.
statements.explanation: Sentence rhythm, favorite words, and typical subjects are all patterns. The imitation can be convincing on the surface and hollow underneath, because the model has none of the author's intentions. Treat it as pastiche and say so if you publish it.

statements.text: When a model writes about grief, it is drawing on its own experience of loss.
statements.explanation: The model has no experiences. It produces text shaped by how people have written about grief. The writing can still move a reader, because the patterns came from people who felt it. The feeling in the text is borrowed, not lived.

statements.text: A model has personal taste and knows which of its drafts your readers will like best.
statements.explanation: A model can rank drafts against criteria you give it, and that is useful for a first cut. It has no audience, no stakes, and no taste of its own. Reader response is something you test with readers, or judge yourself.

statements.text: Asking a model to critique a draft gives useful prompts for revision, not a verdict on the work.
statements.explanation: A critique pass can flag unclear passages, pacing problems, and overused words. It can also invent problems or praise weak work, especially if it senses what you want to hear. Use it as a second reader whose notes you weigh, not obey.

statements.text: Editing generated text is unnecessary because the model already chose the best wording.
statements.explanation: The model chose likely wording, which tends toward the generic. Editing is where specificity, voice, and accuracy come in. Readers notice flat phrasing even when they cannot name it. A generated draft is raw material, not a finished piece.

statements.text: Generated text tends toward common phrasing and structure, so editing for specific detail is what makes it read as yours.
statements.explanation: Likely words are familiar words. Replacing a general claim with a concrete example, cutting stock transitions, and adding what only you know are the edits that turn a competent draft into a distinctive one.

statements.text: The first draft a model produces is as good as the result will get; re-prompting cannot improve it.
statements.explanation: Revision prompts are where most of the value is: tighten this, give an example here, change the opening, remove the cliches. Each round narrows toward what you want. Treating the first output as final skips the part that makes it good.

statements.text: Using a model for brainstorming and then writing the piece yourself is a common way to keep your own voice.
statements.explanation: The model widens the field of options and spots gaps; you write the sentences. The result carries your judgment and rhythm, and disclosure is simple because the published words are yours. Many writers and editors recommend exactly this split.

statements.text: Using AI anywhere in a creative process makes the whole work AI-generated.
statements.explanation: There is a wide range between a spell checker, a brainstorming partner, a drafted paragraph, and a fully generated piece. Honest disclosure describes what the tool did. Policies at publishers and competitions usually draw lines by the kind of help, not by any use at all.

statements.text: Many publishers, competitions, and schools require you to say when AI was used in a piece of work.
statements.explanation: Rules differ, but disclosure is the common thread. Some venues bar generated text entirely; others allow it with a note; most expect honesty about the process. Read the policy before submitting, and keep a record of how you used the tool.

statements.text: Text a model generated for you can be published under your name anywhere without disclosure.
statements.explanation: Many venues treat undisclosed AI text as a breach of their rules, and some readers treat it as a breach of trust. Where disclosure is required, silence can mean retraction or disqualification. Where it is not, a brief note still protects your credibility.

statements.text: In some countries, a work produced entirely by a model with no human creative input cannot be copyrighted.
statements.explanation: Copyright offices and courts in several jurisdictions have held that authorship requires a human. Works where a person selected, arranged, or substantially edited the output are treated differently. The rules vary by country and are still being worked out.

statements.text: Anything a model produces is automatically yours to copyright.
statements.explanation: Ownership of generated output depends on the country, the tool's terms of service, and how much human creative input was involved. Several authorities refuse registration for purely machine-made works. Assume nothing; check the terms and the local rules before relying on it.

statements.text: Whether training a model on copyrighted works is lawful is contested and differs by country.
statements.explanation: Cases are moving through courts, and legislatures have taken different positions on text and data mining. Outcomes may differ for research and commercial use. For creative professionals the practical question is what a given tool's terms say about training and output.

statements.text: A model will refuse to copy a copyrighted work, so its output is always safe to use.
statements.explanation: Refusals are a filter, not a guarantee. Models can reproduce memorized passages, lyrics, or near-identical images when prompted in certain ways, and filters miss cases. For published work, check distinctive passages and images against their likely sources.

statements.text: A few seconds of recorded speech can be enough for a model to imitate a person's voice.
statements.explanation: Voice cloning tools work from short samples, which is why consent and labeling matter. The same capability restores a voice lost to illness and enables fraud calls. Reputable tools require permission from the person being cloned.

statements.text: Cloning a performer's voice is acceptable as long as you credit the performer.
statements.explanation: Credit does not substitute for consent. A person's voice and likeness are protected in many places, and performers' unions and platforms have rules about synthetic voices. The right order is permission first, then credit, then release.

statements.text: Generated images carry no risk of showing a real person, because models cannot reproduce faces.
statements.explanation: Models reproduce faces well, and public figures appear often enough in training data to be rendered on request. That is the basis of deepfakes. Responsible tools block named individuals, and responsible users do not try to get around the block.

statements.text: Some tools attach labels or hidden watermarks to generated images, and those marks can be lost when a file is edited or re-saved.
statements.explanation: Content credentials and watermarks help platforms and viewers identify generated media. Cropping, screenshots, and format changes can strip them. They raise the bar; they do not settle the question. Provenance still rests on the person who publishes.

statements.text: Every AI image tool labels its output as generated, so viewers can always tell.
statements.explanation: Labeling is uneven: some tools add marks by default, some offer it as an option, and some add nothing. Marks that are added can be removed. Viewers should treat striking images with the same skepticism they apply to striking claims.

statements.text: Image generators can get details wrong, such as the text on a sign, the number of fingers, or the count of objects in a scene.
statements.explanation: The model optimizes for overall plausibility, and small structured details are where that breaks. Newer systems do better, and errors still slip through. Look closely at text, hands, reflections, and counts before using an image for anything that matters.

statements.text: Image models learn from large collections of pictures paired with captions, which is why describing a scene in caption-like language works well.
statements.explanation: The training signal is the link between words and images. Prompts that name the subject, setting, medium, lighting, and mood map onto what the model learned. Abstract instructions such as make it better give it little to work with.

statements.text: Longer and more detailed image prompts always produce better pictures.
statements.explanation: Detail helps up to the point where instructions conflict or the model loses track. Past that, extra words add noise, and the model picks which to honor. A focused prompt with the few details that matter usually beats an exhaustive one.

statements.text: The same image prompt gives the same picture every time.
statements.explanation: Generation starts from random noise, so repeated runs produce different images unless the tool lets you fix the random seed. That variation is useful for exploring. When you need to reproduce a result, save the seed and settings along with the prompt.

statements.text: Details such as medium, lighting, era, and camera angle in a prompt change the look of a generated image.
statements.explanation: Each term pulls the output toward images that were captioned that way. Watercolor, overcast light, a specific decade, or a low angle all shift the result predictably. Learning a small vocabulary of these terms gives you steering control.

statements.text: A model translation can keep the meaning of a poem while losing its rhyme, rhythm, or wordplay unless you ask it to prioritize them.
statements.explanation: Translation involves trade-offs, and the model makes them by default toward literal meaning. Asking for a version that keeps the meter, or offering several versions with different priorities, puts the trade-off back in your hands.

statements.text: Creative AI tools only work in English, so prompts in other languages produce nothing useful.
statements.explanation: Most large models handle many languages, and image tools accept prompts in many languages. Quality is uneven and usually best in languages with the most training data. For non-English work, test the tool on your language before relying on it.

statements.text: Models invent genuinely new art movements on their own.
statements.explanation: A model recombines what exists. The striking new combinations come from a person's prompts, selection, and framing. Movements form when people adopt, argue over, and extend a style, which is social work that a model does not do.

statements.text: Generating many options and discarding most of them is a normal part of working creatively with a model.
statements.explanation: The cost of a bad draft is near zero, so the workflow shifts toward volume and selection. Most outputs will be ordinary. The value is in the one or two that spark something, and in the judgment that recognizes them.

statements.text: A person should review generated creative content before it is published, the same way Praxis reviews every page.
statements.explanation: Human oversight is one of the Praxis principles: no AI output goes live without a person reading it. For creative work the review catches errors of fact, tone, and taste, and it makes the publisher accountable for what went out.

statements.text: Because models cannot copy, every idea they produce is original.
statements.explanation: Models can reproduce memorized text and closely imitate well-represented images, and their typical ideas are, by construction, the common ones. Originality comes from what you ask, what you select, and what you change. Check distinctive output before claiming it as new.
